```{r}
source("R/book.R")

n_vehicles <- dd$n_rows[1]
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Draft"}
This book is a working draft. Chapters marked **To be written** are placeholders

## What this book is for

The CARS project (*Connecting Administrative vehicle data for Research on
Sustainable transport*) has combined three open government datasets, the MOT
test results, the MOT history of every vehicle, and the DVLA's vehicle
records, into one research-ready table. It describes
`r fmt_m(n_vehicles)` vehicles that were on the roads of the United Kingdom at
some point between 2005 and 2025. For each vehicle it gives the make, model,
fuel, engine size, emissions standard and other characteristics, and, for
every year, how far the vehicle was driven and in which postcode area it was
tested.

Data like this has not been available before. The UK publishes counts of
licensed vehicles, but not how much vehicles are used, area by area, or how the
fleet in a place changes as vehicles arrive, age, move away and are scrapped.
The CARS data makes those questions answerable, for example:

- How far are cars driven in different parts of the country, and is that
  changing?
- How quickly are electric vehicles spreading, and where do they go once their
  first owner sells them?
- How many older diesel vehicles remain in an area that is considering a Clean
  Air Zone?
- How long do vehicles last, and how does their use change with age?

The source data was collected for administration, not research. Making sense of
it needs some knowledge of how vehicles are tested, registered and classified in
the UK, and an understanding of what the data can and cannot tell you. This book
provides both.

## Who it is for

The book is written for researchers, analysts and policymakers who are
intelligent and numerate but not necessarily experts on vehicles or on
administrative data. It supports two ways of working:

::: {.callout-tip title="Working in a spreadsheet"}
Most questions can be answered from the **aggregate tables**: CSV files of
counts and mileage by postcode area, year, vehicle type and fuel, which open
in Excel or any spreadsheet. @sec-aggregate-tables describes them and
@sec-examples-spreadsheet works through examples.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Working in code"}
The **vehicle table** (`vehicles_enhanced.parquet`) has one row per vehicle and
is around 9 GB. It is far too large for a spreadsheet, but on an ordinary
laptop it can be queried in seconds with DuckDB from R, Python or the command
line. @sec-vehicle-table describes it and @sec-examples-code works through
examples.
:::

## How the book is organised

**Part I, Background**, explains the vehicle data system in the UK: what an MOT
test is (@sec-mot-test), which organisations hold which data
(@sec-data-landscape), how vehicles are classified (@sec-vehicle-types), fuels
and emissions standards (@sec-fuels-emissions), number plates
(@sec-number-plates), the life of a vehicle from registration to scrapping
(@sec-lifecycle) and the geography the data uses (@sec-geography). Readers who
know the field can skip it, but the chapters on the life of a vehicle and on
geography explain features of the data that catch out even experienced
analysts.

**Part II, The CARS data**, describes where the data comes from and how it was
built (@sec-sources-linkage, @sec-pipeline), what is published
(@sec-data-products), the vehicle table and the aggregate tables in detail
(@sec-vehicle-table, @sec-aggregate-tables), and how well the data compares
with official statistics (@sec-data-quality).

**Part III, Using the data**, gathers the concepts and pitfalls you need to
know before analysing the data (@sec-pitfalls), shows how to get started
(@sec-getting-started), and works through examples in a spreadsheet and in
code.

The **appendices** hold a glossary, the full data dictionary, a catalogue of
the aggregate tables, notes on how this book is maintained, and the technical
reports produced by the data pipeline.

::: {.callout-important title="Read this before you start"}
If you read only one chapter, read @sec-pitfalls. The most common mistakes
with this data are not technical: treating where a vehicle was *tested* as
where it is *kept*, reading the fall in vehicle numbers in the last few years
as a real decline, or comparing averages built on different groups of
vehicles.
:::

## The CARS project

CARS is funded by [ADR UK](https://www.adruk.org/) and runs from July 2022 to
March 2027. It is a collaboration between the University of Leeds, the
University of Bristol and an independent consultant. See the
[project website](https://cars-project.github.io/) for the team, events and
news.
